I am 36 years old and have farmed my 10.1 mu in Quzhou County for 15 years. I never went to school, but I learned farming from my father and from watching what works on my land. My household has six people, and some of my family work off-farm, so I need to manage my crops efficiently without wasting labor or money. I have a well, so water is not my biggest worry.

For my wheat, I will sow in early October after the National Day holiday. I will rotary till the field first to prepare a good seedbed. I use improved wheat seed — I usually buy what my neighbors buy, varieties like Jimai 22 or Lumai, because they are reliable here. For fertilizer, I will spread compound fertilizer as a basal application before sowing, and then topdress with urea in spring when the wheat turns green and starts jointing. I have learned that if I don't feed the wheat enough nitrogen in spring, the heads will be small. I will irrigate three times: once before winter to help the wheat survive the cold, once at jointing, and once during grain filling. I will spray pesticides about four times — for weeds, insects, and to prevent disease when the weather is humid. I expect my wheat to yield about 1000 jin per mu, which is what I usually get.

For my maize, I sow right after wheat harvest in early June. I never till for maize — I sow directly into the wheat stubble. This saves time and labor, and the stubble helps keep moisture. I always use hybrid seed, usually Denghai or Nongda varieties, because they give higher yields. I apply compound fertilizer at sowing as a basal dose. I may add a little urea later if the leaves look yellow. I irrigate twice: once after sowing if the soil is dry, and once at the big trumpet stage when the maize needs the most water. I spray pesticides three times, mainly for insects and weeds. I expect my maize to yield around 1100 jin per mu, maybe more if the summer rains come at the right time.
